tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

schema.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
schema.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
schema.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

content.content:
# SYSTEM DESCRIPTION:

OneSport is dedicated to offering up-to-date and pertinent information on a wide range of sports and athletic events. 
Our primary aim is to keep fans and enthusiasts well-informed and engaged. 
The project strives to serve as a one-stop destination for comprehensive sports news, event updates, and a convenient platform for purchasing tickets to various sporting events.

# USER STORIES:

1) As a User, I want to be able to signup in order to have an account 
2) As a User, I want to be able to login
3) As a User, I want to logout from the account by clicking on the Navbar
4) As a User, I want to be able to have access to my profile settings
5) As a User, I want to be able to delete my account by clicking on a button from the profile settings page
6) As a User, I want to be able to modify my email and password in order to change my credentials
7) As a User, I want to see all recent news
8) As a User, I want to filter Italian news by selecting from the menu of available countries 
9) As a User, I want to add to my favourite news all the news I'm interested in, in order to read them later
10) As a User, I want to delete from my favourite news all the news that I'm no longer interested 
11) As a User, I want to see available tickets for upcoming sporting events

content.text:
I've read the task and the 24 OneSport stories. Here is my triage, and then I want your pushback before we go further.

**Noise, keep out of the architecture discussion.** Stories 3 (logout on the navbar), 4 (access profile settings), 20, 21, 22 (view lists you already have). These are UI placement or read views of data other stories already create. They add nothing to the design.

**Commodity, note once and move on.** Stories 1, 2, 6 (signup, login, change credentials). Every system has them. The only one with architectural teeth is story 5, delete account. It forces a cascade decision: what happens to your friendships, pending requests, and saved items. That is one sentence in the design, not a driver.

**The nuggets of gold, in order of how much they shape the architecture:**

1. **News and tickets come from outside.** Stories 7, 8, 11, 12. There is no admin story, no editor, no "publish an event" story anywhere. Nobody in OneSport writes news or creates events. So the content has to be aggregated from external sources. That is the single largest decision: ingestion, caching, freshness, rate limits, and normalising different providers into one schema. The country filter in 8 and 12 tells us the normalised schema needs a country attribute, which many feeds will not give you cleanly.

2. **Users save references to things OneSport does not own.** Stories 9, 10, 13, 14, 15. Favourite news and ticket collections point at external, volatile items. A news article gets taken down, a ticket sells out, an event is cancelled. Do we store a snapshot or a reference? This decides your data model and your consistency story.

3. **A small social graph.** Stories 16, 17, 18, 19, 23, 24. Friend requests with a pending state, bidirectional friendship, and lookup by email. This is the only user-generated relational data in the system. It is small, but it is a different shape from the rest and it has a privacy angle: lookup by email means account enumeration.

**One thing that bothers me.** The system description promises "purchasing tickets", but no story actually purchases anything. Story 13 only says "in order to purchase them later". I would read this as purchase is out of scope or a redirect to the vendor, which means no payments, no inventory, no orders. That drops a huge amount of complexity. Do you agree with reading it that way, or do you want to treat purchase as in scope?

message.content:
<!-- attach: /Users/jurajpetras/school-mag/vibecoding/AI4SE_Labs_2026/Week_05_Designing/Tasks/data/OneSport.txt:L5 -->
> and a convenient platform for purchasing tickets to various sporting events

I read this part as if this platform should support purchasing tickets.

Also to your points where things "come from outside" or "OneSport does not own", I don't actually read any of the points this way. I think the goal for the product is to have everything within it. It will be a sports news site where you can see everything sports + be able to purchase tickets.

Am I misreading something?

content.text:
You are not misreading the description. You are reading the stories differently from me, and the stories themselves do not settle it. Let me separate the two points.

**Purchasing tickets.** The description says it plainly, you are right. My hesitation was only that no story exercises it, which is odd for the most complex feature in the product. But a system description is a requirement too, and "purchase later" in story 13 only makes sense if purchase exists. I will treat purchase as in scope. That brings in three things the stories never mention but which must exist: ticket inventory with a finite count, an order or purchase record, and a payment step. Those three will shape the architecture more than anything else in the list, because they are the only part where correctness really matters. Two people buying the last seat is a real bug. A favourite being stale is not.

**Where content comes from.** Here I inferred from absence, and absence is weak evidence. The story list is entirely "As a User", so it may simply omit the staff side rather than imply there is none. If OneSport owns everything, then someone inside OneSport has to write the news, create the events, and define the tickets. That means an admin or editor role and a content management side that is nowhere in the 24 stories. That is fine, but we should write it down as an explicit assumption, because it changes the system from a thin aggregator into a real three-part product: a content system, a ticket shop, and a social layer.

So under your reading the real drivers become:

1. Ticket purchase: inventory, orders, concurrency, and payment.
2. Content authored in-house: an admin side the stories do not show, which means we design for it anyway.
3. Personal collections and the small social graph, which stay as I described, but with the "volatile external item" worry gone since we own the items.

One decision before we move on. Payment itself: do we assume an external payment provider handles the card and OneSport only records the order, or do you want to keep payment abstract and out of the discussion? I would take the provider route, since it is what every real system does and it introduces an interesting failure mode, the webhook that arrives after the user has closed the tab.

message.content:
As this assignment is about designing the architecture I think we should include everything, it will make the design more interesting. I think decision about the payment provider / infrastructure should be part of the design itself.

For the editor / admin writing news stories, I think this is a bad direction to go. They should have an ability to do so, but for a product like this that isn't very feasible. If this was something that wanted to actually exist and satisfy the description, it should have everything. We can't expect all the sports event organizers to go through our platform. Therefore some events might just redirect to the external ticket purchase page. A lot of new might be automatically pulled in from the official sources or other new sites but editors should be able to edit / add some as well.

Does this make sense? Would you change anything?

content.text:
Yes, it makes sense, and it is actually the most honest reading of the description. I would keep it and sharpen one thing.

**What you are describing is a hybrid on both axes.** News is partly ingested from feeds and partly authored by editors. Tickets are partly sold natively and partly a redirect to an external vendor. That is how a real product in this space would look, and it is the version worth designing.

**The one sharpening.** The hybrid should not become two parallel systems. The way to avoid that is to decide early that there is one news model and one event model, each with a source dimension. An article is an article whether a feed pulled it in or an editor wrote it. An event has tickets that are either sold here, with inventory, or fulfilled elsewhere, with a URL. The reader, the favourites, the country filter, the friends who share things: none of them should care where the item came from. If we get that right, the hybrid costs us an ingestion pipeline and a fulfilment mode flag. If we get it wrong, every feature has to be built twice.

**One consequence worth naming now.** Ingestion adds a class of work that has no user in front of it: scheduled fetching, deduplication across sources, and normalising country and sport. That is the first piece of the system that is not a request and response, and it will push every architecture we discuss towards having some kind of background worker. That is good, because it makes the three architectures differ in interesting ways rather than only in how the HTTP layer is sliced.

**One question before we lock the drivers.** When a feed pulls in an article, does it go live immediately, or does it land in a queue for an editor to approve? Automatic is simpler. A review queue adds a moderation state and a small editorial workflow, but it is what a site that calls itself a destination would probably want. I lean towards automatic for most sources with an editor able to hide or edit after the fact, since that keeps the pipeline simple and still gives editors control. Which do you want?

message.content: For the ingest some editorial involvement might be necessary. For some things however automatic makes the most sense. For example player stats could be pulled from the official FIFA site or whatever. Nobody probably needs to manually approve that. With this we have to be very careful that the design doesn't cause a combinatorial explosion of features. Basically having everything implemented n^2 times where n is the number of different variations like (does it require editor approval, does it do X, does it do Y...). We should also make sure that the architecture doesn't create sparse software, where most of the code is not executed.

content.text:
Good concern, and it has a clean answer: the variation goes into data, not into code.

**One pipeline, policy on the source.** Every ingested item flows through the same path: fetch, normalise, deduplicate, store. The only decision is the state the item lands in, published or pending review. That decision is a field on the source configuration, not a branch in the feature code. The FIFA feed is configured as auto-publish, a third-party news site as review. The editor tools then operate on items, not on sources: an editor can edit, hide, or approve any item regardless of how it arrived. So the matrix you fear, approval times origin times fulfilment, collapses to one pipeline plus one state machine on the item, and the combinations exist only as rows in a config table.

**The rule for sparse software.** Do not build a generic plugin framework for sources. Each source gets one small, concrete adapter whose only job is to turn the provider's format into our model. The adapters are the only place where code multiplies, and they multiply linearly with the number of sources, which is exactly the growth you want. Everything downstream is written once. The same discipline applies to tickets: native versus redirect is a fulfilment mode on the event, and only the checkout step looks at it. Favourites, filters, and friends never see it.

**One thing you introduced that I want to pin down.** Player stats are a new kind of content. Articles and events are two content types. Stats are structured tabular data with a different shape, different queries, and a different display. Adding them as a third type is legitimate but it widens the model. My recommendation is to keep two content types, news and events, and use the FIFA example only as the canonical case of an auto-publish source feeding news. If you want stats as a real type we should say so now, because it changes how we judge each architecture. Which do you prefer?

message.content: Actually let's leave out player stats for now. I said that as an example, but it will add some complexity to the injest and data pipeline, where for this type of data we don't want to show all of them, just the "latest version".

content.text:
Agreed, and your reason is the right one. Articles and events are append-only, each arrival is a new item. Stats would be upsert-the-latest, which is a different write pattern and a different idea of what "the item" is. Keeping that out keeps the ingestion pipeline one-shaped. We can note it as a known extension and leave it there.

That gives us the final set of drivers. Here is what I would lock as the architectural requirements, everything else in the 24 stories being commodity or UI detail:

1. **Two content types, news and events,** each with a source dimension. Items arrive either by ingestion or by an editor, and nothing downstream cares which.
2. **An ingestion pipeline** with per-source policy: scheduled fetch, concrete adapter per source, normalise to one schema including country and sport, deduplicate, land as published or pending according to the source config. This is the first background, non-request workload in the system.
3. **An editorial role** that is not in the stories but must exist: create, edit, hide, approve. One set of tools acting on items regardless of origin.
4. **Ticket purchase** with two fulfilment modes on the event: native, meaning inventory, orders, concurrency on the last seat, and a payment provider integration whose choice is part of the design; or redirect, meaning a URL and nothing else.
5. **Personal collections** of news and tickets, including the "clear all" from story 15. Simple, but they reference items that editors can hide and events that can sell out, so we need a stance on what the user sees then.
6. **A small social graph:** pending requests, bidirectional friendship, lookup by email with the enumeration concern, and the cascade when an account is deleted.
7. **Auth and accounts** as commodity.

Two assumptions to carry: the matrix of variations lives in configuration and item state, never in duplicated feature code, and stats are a deliberate exclusion.

If you are happy with this list, the next step inside task 1 is to put the first architecture on the table and take it apart. Tell me when you want that, or change anything above first.

message.content: Actually please come up with 3 or 4 architectures, present them just at the high level, let's discuss them on the high level - basically just through the main few systems (social, purchasing, news) and when we will pick one we can inspect it more in detail

content.text:
Here are four, each described through the three main systems plus where the background ingestion lives.

**A. Modular monolith.** One codebase, one deployment, one relational database. Content, ingestion, commerce, social, and accounts are separate modules with enforced boundaries, but they share the process and the database. News: adapters and the pipeline are the same code, run in a second worker process that pulls jobs from a queue table or Redis. Purchasing: inventory, orders, and the payment call live in the same transaction space as everything else, so the last-seat problem is a row lock. Social: plain tables with foreign keys, friendship is a join table. Trade-off: simplest to build and reason about, strongest consistency for free. The pain is discipline. Nothing stops the social module from reaching into order tables, and the ingestion worker and the web tier scale together whether you want them to or not.

**B. Domain services.** Three or four services split by the domains we identified: content with its ingestion worker, commerce, social together with identity, each owning its own database. A gateway or backend-for-frontend assembles pages. Services talk asynchronously through a message broker: content publishes "article published" and "event changed", commerce publishes "order completed". News: the content service is almost a standalone product, which fits the hybrid source model well. Purchasing: isolated, which is exactly where you want isolation since it holds money and the strictest invariants. Social: small and cheap, but it needs user identity, so it leans on the identity service. Trade-off: scaling and ownership are clean, but every cross-domain feature such as "show my saved tickets with current availability" becomes a network call and a question about staleness. Collections, which cut across news and tickets, have no obvious home.

**C. Event log with read models.** Every change, whether ingested, edited, ordered, or befriended, is appended to a central event stream. Separate consumers build purpose-shaped read models: the recent news feed, the per-country index, the user's collections, the friend list. News: ingestion is just another producer, so the one-pipeline idea becomes literal. Purchasing: the one place that cannot be eventually consistent, so commerce keeps a strongly consistent store and emits events after commit. Social: trivially fits, but gains nothing from it. Trade-off: beautiful fit for ingestion and feeds, excellent audit trail, and read models can be rebuilt. The pain is two consistency models in one system, and a lot of plumbing for the social and account parts that are too small to need it.

**D. Compose managed services.** Buy most of it. A hosted auth provider for accounts. A headless CMS for editorial news and the review queue. The payment provider's hosted checkout for native tickets, with inventory kept in a small custom service. Scheduled cloud functions as the ingestion adapters, writing into the CMS or the content store. A thin custom backend for collections and social, the only parts no vendor sells. Trade-off: fastest to a working product and the least code to own. The pain is that the seams are vendor seams. The country filter across CMS content and ingested content, and the last-seat invariant between the payment provider and our inventory, both end up being integration problems rather than code you control.

A rough map of where each is strong:

| | News and ingestion | Purchasing | Social and collections |
|---|---|---|---|
| A Monolith | fine | strongest | easiest |
| B Services | good | isolated well | awkward |
| C Event log | best | needs an island | overkill |
| D Managed | good | vendor seam | custom anyway |

My lean is A with the ingestion worker deployed separately, possibly borrowing the one good idea from C, an internal domain event table, so the design has somewhere to grow. But I would rather you pick the two or three you find interesting and we argue about them.

message.content:
I'd rule out D completely - it would be a nightmare.
Now for the other three let's discuss them, let's first discuss them from the point of purchasing because that is the most complex part here. content.text:
Agreed on D. And agreed on the framing: the pay step is easy, the hold is the whole problem. Let me first pin the shape of the problem, because it is the same under all three, and then show where they actually differ.

**The shape of the problem.** Contention is not about total volume. It is about one event, one row, one counter that thousands of requests want to decrement in the same second. Horizontal scaling does nothing for that, because you are scaling compute while the bottleneck is a single piece of data. So every architecture ends up with the same three ingredients:

- A hold with a time to live. Reserve, get ten minutes, pay or the hold evaporates. Expiry is a background sweep, not a user action.
- Serialised writes per event. Someone has to be the single decision point for "is there one left". Either a database lock on the inventory row, an atomic counter in memory, or one consumer that owns that event.
- Keeping the herd away from the hot path. Most of the thousands are refreshing availability, not buying. Reads come from a cache with a short time to live and an approximate count. Only a reserve click touches the counter.

Now the three.

**A, monolith.** The natural implementation is a row lock: begin transaction, select the inventory row for update, check, decrement, insert the hold, commit. This is correct and simple, and a decent database will do a few thousand of these per second on one row if the transaction is tiny. The pain is the convoy. Under a real spike the waiting transactions pile up, they each hold a connection from the pool, and because the web tier is shared, the news pages and the friend list start timing out too. One hot event degrades the whole site. The fix is either to move the counter into Redis with an atomic decrement and write the hold to the database afterward, or to put a queue in front of reserve requests. Both are bolt-ons that fight the monolith's instinct of doing everything in one request.

**B, services.** Commerce is its own service with its own database, so the blast radius is contained: the news site stays up while the ticket shop is on fire. That is the real win. Inside the service you have exactly the same choice as in A, and the same hot row. Scaling the commerce service to twenty replicas does not help the counter, it just makes twenty replicas queue at the database. The extra cost is that the event listing lives in the content service and shows availability from the commerce service, so you need either a cross-service call per page or an availability number pushed over the broker and accepted as slightly stale. Stale is fine here, but it has to be a deliberate decision.

**C, event log.** This is where the textbook answer becomes the natural one. A reserve click does not try to decrement anything. It appends a "reservation requested" event. One consumer per event partition reads those in order, holds the counter in memory, and decides yes or no deterministically. There is no contention because there is only one writer per event by construction, and the log in front of it is the queue that absorbs the spike. Expiry, payment confirmed, and release are all further events on the same stream. The pain is that the user's click is now asynchronous. The page has to say "you are in line" and then learn the answer, by polling or a push channel. And the commerce island still needs a strongly consistent store for orders and payments, so in practice the log is the ingress queue and the serialiser, not the system of record.

**Where this leaves us.** All three solve the hot event with the same idea, a single writer per event behind a queue. In C that idea is the architecture. In A and B it is a component you add, and A adds it under more pressure because the hot path shares a process with everything else.

The question that decides a lot: are you willing to make the reserve click asynchronous, "you are in the queue, we will tell you", for hot events? If yes, C's model fits and can even be embedded as a component inside A or B. If the click must answer synchronously, you are committed to the row lock or Redis counter and you accept the convoy risk and mitigate it with rate limiting.

message.content: We need to consider the reality of the situation here. A queue does not solve the problem, it only defers the problem. If the reservation is asynchronous and we get a spike, people might get impatient, refresh, click again, that pushes a new event and and again and again. The queue will delay the problem. + with a queue we will get potentially thousands of connections polling or waiting for update events on their request. Something needs to keep track of those requests. You are right that distribution doesn't help here. We could possibly distribute events, where each event would have the server elsewhere so that we load balance between events, but each event itself can't be distributed. What if we keep this event reservation system simple? Make it a simple API service with a sqlite database on a local drive within the server. No network calls and we still get ACID.

content.text:
I think that is the right instinct, and it is better than my C. Let me say why, then where it bites, because it does bite in two places.

**Why it is right.** Your critique of the queue is correct: a queue converts a contention problem into a state-tracking problem and adds the duplicate-click storm on top. The only real defence against re-clicks is idempotency, one hold per user per event enforced by a unique constraint, and that works regardless of queue or no queue. Once you have that, the question is just how fast the single writer can answer. SQLite on a local SSD answers a tiny transaction in well under a millisecond. There is no connection pool, no network round trip, no lock convoy across processes, because SQLite's one-writer-at-a-time is exactly the serialisation we wanted, enforced by the engine instead of by us. A genuine buying spike for one event is a few thousand reserve attempts per second at the very worst, and that is inside what one box does with WAL mode and a sane fsync setting. The request returns synchronously in milliseconds, so there is nothing to poll for. The hold expiry is an in-process timer over one table. This is a small, boring, correct component. That is what you want holding the money path.

**Where it bites, first: the box is now the single point.** The machine owns the truth about who holds what and how many are sold. If it dies, the holds can die with them, that is acceptable, they were ten-minute promises anyway. The sales cannot. So the design needs a rule: a confirmed sale is written to SQLite and then pushed to the central order store, and the SQLite file is continuously shipped off-box, WAL replication to object storage is the standard trick. On recovery you rebuild from the shipped file, reconcile against the central order store, and reopen. Until then that event is simply not on sale, which is an honest failure mode. You also get a mapping to maintain: which box serves which event. Hot events get a dedicated box, cold events share one, and that mapping lives in the central database as plain configuration. That is your "distribute between events, never within one", made concrete.

**Where it bites, second: the box's bottleneck is not SQLite.** With thousands of people on one event, the limit becomes accepting TLS connections and parsing HTTP, not the database. So the reservation service must not face the public internet. An edge in front does TLS, authentication, rate limiting per user, and routes by event id to the right box. Availability reads never reach the box at all, they come from a cache the box updates every second or so. The box receives only authenticated reserve, release, and confirm calls. Kept that lean, one small machine per hot event is comfortable.

**The payment seam.** Hold is created, the user is sent to the provider, the provider calls a webhook when paid. The webhook handler calls the box to convert the hold into a sale. The ugly case is the webhook arriving after the ten minutes expired and the seat was given to someone else. The standard answer is a short grace period on holds that have a payment in progress, and a refund path for the rare miss. That is a business rule, but the architecture needs the "payment started" state on the hold to make it possible.

**How this maps to the three architectures.** It is really B's commerce service, built deliberately as a single-node, per-event allocator instead of a scaled stateless service, and it fits equally well as the one separately deployed component inside an otherwise monolithic A. It makes C unnecessary for purchasing. Whichever we choose for the rest, this component stays the same.

One decision to confirm: are you comfortable with "the event is off sale until the box recovers" as the failure mode, with sales protected by replication and holds accepted as lost? The alternative is a hot standby per box, which doubles the hardware and adds a failover protocol for very little gain at this scale.

message.content:
I think your critique of sqlite is unfounded here. If the main database goes down the service goes down. Obviously. It doesn't matter if it's sqlite, redis, or a queue.

I agree that it would not be good if the box was the place where TLS termination happened. It would make much more sense to have one primary web service, that can be easily horizontally scaled, it would have one database for news and stuff like that. + it would call this reservation service for any client requests.

Let's say if we have 5 replicas of A, each can even batch these requests and send them in batches to the reservation service.

This way we can easily scale the web layer, while keeping the contended system single threaded.

For the payment system there is not much we can do there. I would use a payment provider like stripe or something similar honestly, but that doesn't matter too much as the interface can be abstracted away. I agree with the grace period and refund policy you mentioned there. But that has nothing to do with the architecture. These web hooks for the payments would probably still come to the primary web instance which would then forward them to the service unless you have a better idea there.

content.text:
Fair, I overstated it. A managed database with a replica fails over faster than a box with a local file, but the event is off sale either way while it is failing over, and the sales are safe in both as long as the file is shipped off-box. It is a difference of recovery time, not of kind. Dropped.

**The shape you describe is now clear and I agree with it.** A horizontally scaled web service, one main database for news, accounts, collections, and social, and the reservation service as the one deliberately single-threaded component that the web tier calls. The web tier owns the public surface: TLS, sessions, rate limits, the availability cache. The box owns one thing, the truth about seats.

**On batching, one caution and one suggestion.** Batching is a genuine throughput win for SQLite specifically, because the cost of a commit is the fsync, not the rows. One transaction covering fifty holds costs about the same as one transaction covering one. So under a spike, batches turn the box's ceiling from thousands of commits per second into tens of thousands of holds per second. The caution is that batching adds a wait window on every replica and you now have a buffer of pending requests on each replica, which is the same state-tracking problem as the queue in miniature, just bounded and short. The suggestion that keeps the code from forking into two paths: make the box's API batch-shaped from the start. It takes a list of reservation requests and returns a list of per-item results. A single click is a batch of one. A replica under load can coalesce whatever arrived in the last few milliseconds into one call. Same endpoint, same code, batching becomes a tuning knob rather than a feature. Keep the connections persistent, one long-lived channel per replica, so there is no connection cost per call either.

**On webhooks, yes, and one addition.** The provider must call something with a public address and a verified signature, which is the web tier. The web tier verifies and forwards a confirm to the box. Two things make that robust and both are cheap. First, idempotency on both ends, because providers retry and the same confirm must be safe to apply twice. Second, the web tier should record the webhook in the main database before it calls the box. If the box is unreachable at that moment, the record is retried later instead of the payment being lost. That is a small outbox table and a retry loop, and it is the only piece of async plumbing purchasing needs.

**Where the three architectures stand after this.** For purchasing, they have collapsed into one shape: the component above is the same whichever we pick, and the web tier it talks to is A scaled horizontally. B would make the content side a separate service too, and C's event log has no job left here. So the remaining question for A versus B versus C is entirely about the news side and the ingestion pipeline, and about whether social and collections want to live next to news or apart from it.

Shall I lay out news and ingestion under the three next, the same way, or do you want to keep on purchasing a little longer?

content.text:
Here is news and ingestion under the three, with purchasing already fixed as the web tier plus the reservation box.

**First, the shape of this workload, because it is the opposite of purchasing.** Writes are tiny: a few hundred articles and events a day across all sources, arriving on a schedule, tolerant of minutes of delay. Reads are large and almost entirely public and identical for everyone: the recent feed, the per-country feed, an article page. The only per-user part is whether an item is in your collection. So the hard parts are not contention. They are caching, the quality of the adapters, deduplication across sources, and the editorial states. Any architecture that makes this workload look complicated is building sparse software.

**A, monolith with a worker role.** The ingestion pipeline is the same codebase started in a second mode: a scheduler fires each source on its interval, the source's adapter fetches and normalises, the shared pipeline deduplicates and writes rows into the main database in the state the source policy says. Editors get admin pages in the same application acting on the same rows. Reads are one indexed query on country, sport, and publish time, and because the pages are public, a CDN or HTTP cache in front of the web tier absorbs the thousands of refreshes during a big match. The pain is small and real: a misbehaving adapter can hammer the main database, and the worker ships with every web deploy whether it changed or not. Both are tolerable at this volume. Collections and social sit in the same database as the articles, so "my saved news" is a join, and "is this in my collection" is a lookup, nothing crosses a boundary.

**B, content as its own service.** Articles, events, ingestion, and the editorial tools become one service with its own database. It is a clean product on its own, and a separate team could own it. The cost shows up immediately in the two features that cut across: collections, which hold article and event ids from the content service and user ids from the identity side, and the event listing, which needs availability from the reservation box. Every one of those pages becomes a batch lookup across a network boundary, with caching and staleness decisions attached. Those are solvable, but we would be solving them to buy an isolation that this workload does not need. The content side has no spike that could hurt the rest. The one place it could, a runaway adapter, is a rate limit on the worker, not a service boundary. B's gain here is organisational, and we do not have the organisation.

**C, event log with read models.** Ingestion emits "article ingested", editors emit "article approved" or "article hidden", consumers build the recent feed and the per-country feed as read models. It fits the one-pipeline idea elegantly and gives rebuildable views and an audit trail for free. But look at what the read models would be: a table indexed by country and time. That is the table A already has. For a few hundred writes a day, the log, the consumers, the rebuild tooling, and the eventual consistency between "editor clicked hide" and "article disappeared" are infrastructure with almost nothing flowing through it. The one thing C offers that A does not, a durable history of every state change, we can get in A with an item history table if we ever want it.

**Social and collections, briefly, since they follow the same logic.** They are small, relational, and per-user. In A they are tables beside everything else and the account-deletion cascade is foreign keys. In B they are the orphan nobody owns. In C they gain nothing.

**My conclusion.** The two workloads that have real architectural weight pull in opposite directions, and the design honours both: purchasing is isolated into a single-threaded box because it must be, and everything else stays in one scaled web tier with one database because splitting it would only add seams. That is A with one deliberate carve-out, and the carve-out is the only place where B's instinct was right.

Are you content to pick that, and then go a level down into it as the task asks? Or do you want to push on B for the content side before we commit?

content.text:
Let me state it plainly, as a list of components, and then deal with the caches and with live stats honestly.

**The proposal: one application, one database, one box for seats.**

1. **Web service.** One codebase, stateless, run as several identical replicas behind a load balancer. It serves everything a user or editor sees: news, events, accounts, collections, social, the editorial admin pages, and the payment webhook endpoint. All public traffic and all TLS end here.
2. **Main database.** One relational database, Postgres. It holds users, articles, events, sources and their policies, collections, friendships, orders, and the webhook outbox. The hot-seat counter is deliberately not here.
3. **Worker.** The same codebase started in worker mode, one instance. It runs the ingestion schedule, one adapter per source, and the retry loop for webhooks that failed to reach the box. It writes into the main database like any other part of the application.
4. **Reservation service.** A separate small program with SQLite on its local disk. It owns holds and sold counts for a set of events. The web replicas talk to it over a persistent connection with the batch-shaped API, it confirms sales when told to, it expires its own holds. Its file is shipped off-box continuously.
5. **Payment provider.** External, behind an interface. Checkout happens on their page, confirmation arrives as a webhook to the web service.

That is five things, and only one of them, the box, is not off the shelf.

**On caches, you caught me building up complexity, so here is the stripped version.** I mentioned a CDN and an availability cache. Drop the CDN. Postgres serving an indexed feed query comfortably handles the news read load of this product, and if that ever stops being true the fix is a read replica, which is still a database and not a cache. What remains is one thing, and I would not call it a cache: the availability number shown on an event page. The rule is that the box is the only truth, and it is consulted on every reserve. The number on the page is a snapshot the web replicas pull from the box roughly once a second and keep in memory. It is allowed to be a second stale, because the only thing it affects is whether a button looks enabled, and the reserve call corrects it. No invalidation exists anywhere, because nothing is ever invalidated. There is a stated staleness bound and a write path that does not trust it. If we later cache news pages, it is the same rule: a short time to live, no invalidation logic, and the accepted consequence that a hidden article may linger for thirty seconds.

**On live stats.** This is a different workload from both of the others. It is upsert-the-latest with fan-out: one source updating a match every few seconds, thousands of viewers wanting to see it. It fits the proposal with one adapter and one addition:

- The adapter is just another worker source, polling the official feed and writing the current match state as one row per match. Same pipeline, auto-publish policy, no editorial step. The row is overwritten, not appended, which is the only new behaviour.
- The fan-out has two versions. The simple one: the match page polls the web service every ten seconds. That is a plain read of one row, the replicas scale horizontally, and many real sports sites do exactly this. The ambitious one: the web replicas hold open connections, server-sent events, and need to learn when a match row changed. That requires one new component, a publish-subscribe channel the worker publishes to and every replica subscribes to. Postgres can do this natively with its notify mechanism, or Redis if the volume grows.

What matters for today's decision is that neither version pulls stats into the main transactional path or into the box. Stats never contend with anything. The proposal does not block the feature, and the ambitious version costs exactly one new component, not a redesign.

Does that answer what you were asking, or is there a part of it you want me to go a level deeper on?

content.text:
**Names.** I will call them the Core Service and the Reservation Service from here on. Core Service is the horizontally scaled application that owns everything except seats. Reservation Service is the single-threaded SQLite program that owns seats.

**The Reservation Service, properly.** You are right that a counter is the degenerate case. Its model is:

- **Event**, with one or more **ticket categories** (tribune, behind the goal, VIP). A category is either a quantity pool, where seats are not individually tracked, or a set of named **seats**. Both are rows in the same tables, a seat is just a category entry with a seat label, and a pool is a category with a count and no labels.
- **Reservation**, the log entry: who, which event, which seats or which category and quantity, created at, expires at, and state. States are held, payment pending, sold, cancelled, expired. Every transition is a row update plus an append to a history table, so there is a record of every seat's life.
- **Uniqueness** is a constraint: a seat label can appear in at most one active reservation for its event. For pools it is a check that held plus sold does not exceed capacity, done inside the same transaction. One user, one active reservation per event, so double clicks return the existing one.

Its API is exactly what you said, and it is deliberately ignorant of money:

| Call | Does |
|---|---|
| reserve(event, items) | validates, creates the hold, returns reservation id and expiry; batch-shaped, a single click is a batch of one |
| mark payment pending(id) | extends the hold slightly and prevents expiry while the provider is in flight |
| confirm(id) | turns held seats into sold, idempotent |
| cancel(id) | releases, idempotent |
| availability(event) | per-category counts and, for seated categories, the free seat list |

Expiry is internal: a timer sweeps holds past their expiry that are not payment pending. The Core Service does the whole payment conversation with the provider and only ever tells the Reservation Service the outcome.

**Live news path.** Agreed, and I retract it for now. One data path: the worker writes rows, the Core Service reads rows, a page that wants to feel live polls. No subscription channel in this design. If a push channel ever becomes necessary, it should be added once, as a single mechanism, and the thing most likely to force it is not stats.

**Chat.** The stories do not ask for it. Stories 16 to 24 are friend requests, accept, refuse, remove, find by email, and see a friend's details. There is no message, no feed, no sharing. The friend list has no stated purpose beyond seeing each other's details, which is odd but it is what is written. I would not invent chat. I would note that the social graph is the natural anchor for a future feature such as messaging or sharing a saved event, and that such a feature would be the real driver for a push channel, which is why we should not build one for stats alone.

**Everything the Core Service handles.** Grouped by area, nothing hidden:

- **Accounts.** Signup, login, session management, change email and password, delete account with the cascade over collections, friendships, pending requests, and orders kept as anonymised records.
- **Content reads.** Recent news, news by country, article page, upcoming events, events by country, event page with the availability snapshot.
- **Editorial.** Role-gated admin pages: create and edit articles and events, approve or hide ingested items, define ticket categories and seats for native events, set the redirect URL for external ones, manage sources and their policies.
- **Ingestion, in worker mode.** Scheduler, one adapter per source, normalisation into one schema, deduplication, writing items in the state the source policy dictates.
- **Collections.** Add, remove, list, clear all, for both news and tickets. Items that were hidden or sold out stay in the list with a flag, so nothing in a user's list silently vanishes.
- **Social.** Send, accept, refuse, and remove, find a user by email with rate limiting so it cannot be used to enumerate accounts, friend list with details.
- **Purchasing orchestration.** Event listing with the snapshot pulled from the Reservation Service, reserve on the user's click, create the provider checkout, receive the signed webhook, write it to the outbox, confirm or cancel at the Reservation Service, record the order, retry the outbox from worker mode, handle the grace and refund rules.
- **Cross-cutting.** Authentication on every request, roles for editors, rate limits, structured logging.

Two notes on that list. Everything in it is request and response except ingestion and outbox retry, which is why a single codebase with a worker mode covers it. And the purchasing orchestration is the only area that talks to anything outside the main database, so it is the only area that needs the outbox and retry discipline.

One ambiguity I would rather you decide than I assume: do we treat "see a friend's details" as the whole social feature and design nothing more, or do you want to assume friends can see each other's saved events, which is the smallest thing that gives the friend list a reason to exist?
